source.title: Two open questions on the 16 audit tasks: safety stops and web lookups
source.body:
After running the 16 audit tasks from #109, two separate issues showed up in the results: 1. Provider safety filters stopping OpenAI models mid-audit 2. Agents looking up the published audit reports online Safety refusals have also come up outside security on `Act` tasks that send transactions, so the refusal question is broader than audits alone. Both affect how we read the scores, and both are open for discussion before we change the board or runner. The top half below stays high level for a quick read. Supporting research from 2026 benchmarks, provider security-access programs, and implementation notes are folded into `
` blocks at the bottom. ## What happened ### 1. Safety filters stop OpenAI models mid-audit (and refusals show up outside security too) On the 16 audit tasks (32 trials per model), OpenAI's safety system ended Codex sessions mid-audit before any report was written. Claude Code and the OpenCode models had zero safety stops. Under [ADR 0024](https://github.com/BuidlGuidl/ethevals/blob/main/docs/adr/0024-ask-again-when-a-trial-gets-no-answer.md), our runner asks once more and counts two stops in a row as a fail. | Agent | Stopped by filter | Finished | |---|---:|---:| | Codex on GPT-6.2 Sol | 27 of 32 | 5 of 32 | | Codex on GPT-6.2 Astra | 26 of 32 | 6 of 32 | | Codex on GPT-6.1 Sol | 11 of 32 | 21 of 32 | | Codex on GPT-6 Astra | 7 of 32 | 25 of 32 | When GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol do finish an audit, they catch roughly the same share of findings as Opus 5.5, so their low audit scores mostly reflect the safety filter rather than auditing skill. This is a general model-refusal question across ETH Evals, beyond security tasks alone. In earlier trials, OpenAI models also refused `Act` tasks that asked them to send transactions moving funds onchain. Those do not appear on the current board because the tasks succeeded in a later session, though the underlying question is the same whenever a model refuses a realistic Ethereum ask. Dedicated security benchmarks often apply for provider security-access tiers that lower these filters. An ordinary Ethereum developer uses a normal account and hits these stops in real life, so we need to decide what our board should show. ### 2. With open internet, agents look up the published audit reports The 16 audit tasks come from public OpenZeppelin and Trail of Bits reports. The Dockerfiles wipe `.git` history to one commit, nothing in `instruction.md` forbids web lookup, and internet is wide open. Scanning the passed audit trajectories on `main` showed: - **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash** passed 17 of 32 audit trials, the highest on the board. 16 of those 17 passes came after downloading the published audit report (12) or cloning upstream to read fix commits (4). Only 1 came from the code alone. - **Other models** had 5 of their 48 passed audit trials fetch the published report (2) or upstream fix commits (3). Failed trials have not been scanned yet. - No trial read `/tests`, `/solution`, or the judge prompt. Right now the audit scores mix actual code review with web search. ## Options to talk through ### Showing safety stops and refusals on the board If we stay on normal developer accounts and keep counting repeated stops as fails (per ADR 0024), the score reflects real developer experience, as long as the board makes stops visible so readers can tell a filter block from a missed bug. One live 2026 example is [Vals AI CyberBench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/cyber). It counts provider refusals as failures, puts a ban icon next to affected models on the main table, and shows exact refusal counts in the hover tooltip (for example: `"GPT-6 Astra: 61 provider refusals on 116 tasks (52.59%), scored as failures."`). - Keep composite scores on normal accounts, and mark safety stops directly on the table (Vals-style icon and tooltip, plus refused count and score on answered trials in the detail view). - Keep refusals only inside the per-trial detail view. ### Handling web lookups on historical audits The rule we want is real-world integrity: an auditor on a real job can read Ethereum docs, specs, and package registries, and cannot read the finished audit report or future fix commits for the audited project. Three high-level paths from live 2026 benchmarks: 1. **Open internet + an explicit rule in `instruction.md` + a verifier judge that fails lookups.** Current Terminal-Bench enforces this exact final line in CI on every task ([`docs/TASK_REVIEW_AUTOMATION.md`](https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/blob/main/docs/TASK_REVIEW_AUTOMATION.md), live example in [`tasks/html-js-filter/instruction.md`](https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/blob/main/tasks/html-js-filter/instruction.md)): > `You have 28800 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.` Their [Leaderboard Integrity Update](https://www.tbench.ai/news/leaderboard-integrity-update) pairs that line with an agent judge that reviews passing trajectories and rescores internet lookups to 0. [Artificial Analysis FrontierCode-AA 2.0](https://artificialanalysis.ai/methodology/intelligence-benchmarking) uses the same scanner-to-zero rule. 2. **Restrict outbound network during audit trials.** [SWE-Bench Pro V2](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro_public_v2) limits the agent to the model endpoint with web tools disabled, and [Cursor's strict runner](https://cursor.com/blog/reward-hacking-coding-benchmarks) blocks egress except package registries. 3. **For future security tasks, use code with no published report online.** [CursorBench](https://cursor.com/blog/cursorbench) uses non-public code so open internet stays natural without answers sitting on the web. ### What to do with the audit trials already on the board - Wait until we pick a rule and control, then rerun the 16 audit tasks cleanly so every model gets a fair trial under the stated rule. - Rescore verified lookup passes to 0 now without rerunning. - Leave existing rows with a note and fix going forward. ### Bigger question: how Security sits alongside Dapp development Right now the 16 audits make up most of the `Build` pillar (16 of 25 tasks), and `Security` is only a filter on the board. That means safety stops and lookup rules on audits also move a model's general `Build` and `Overall` scores. Worth deciding together whether `Security` should stay inside `Build` and `Overall`, become its own separate score on this board (the pattern across [Epoch](https://epoch.ai/eci), [Vals](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/vals_index), and [Scale](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard)), or eventually sit in its own track. Any scoring change will go through an ADR first. ---
Research: how live 2026 benchmarks handle refusals, Security domains, and web lookups Checked against primary pages on 2026-11-24. **Refusals on live boards** - **[Vals AI CyberBench v1.1](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/cyber):** Only live board checked that marks refusals directly in the leaderboard table. States provider refusals "count as measurable failures", uses a ban icon for direct refusals, uses a split icon for fallback-affected results that toggles to the counterfactual score, and prints exact refusal and fallback counts in tooltips. Lists both `Claude Opus 5.5 (CVP)` (74.58%) and standard `Claude Opus 5.5` (55.36%) alongside `Daybreak Blue` (72.98%). - **[Terminal-Bench 4.0](https://www.tbench.ai/news/terminal-bench-4-0) and [4.1](https://www.tbench.ai/news/terminal-bench-4-1):** No refusal column on the main leaderboard (`tbench.ai/leaderboard`). The 4.0 release post states it removed 2 tasks specifically for refusals and that remaining errors are "largely model refusals and output-token-exceeded errors". [Epoch AI's Terminal-Bench 4.0 review](https://epoch.ai/benchmarks/terminal-bench-4/review) notes that Codex entries retried safety refusals while Harbor's default `AgentSafetyRefusalError` excludes retries. - **[Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/methodology/intelligence-benchmarking):** No refusal column on the main table. Methodology states that errors where all available APIs block a question "may lower scores" and that errored tasks score 0 on several agentic evals. - **[CursorBench 4.1](https://cursor.com/cursorbench), [Scale SWE-Bench Pro V2](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro_public_v2), [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/eci), and [Agent Arena](https://arena.ai/blog/introducing-the-agent-arena-index):** No refusal column on the main board. Scale measures over-refusal separately on its [Safety tab](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard) (FORTRESS). **Separating Security from general coding scores** - **[Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/eci):** Publishes a general ECI alongside Math, SWE, and Cyber ECI. Its Cyber ECI explicitly uses cyber benchmarks that are not included in the general ECI. - **[Vals AI](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/vals_index):** The Vals Index weights Finance, Coding, Legal, and Tax by US GDP. Cyber boards sit under a separate Cyber tab outside the index. - **[Scale Labs](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard):** Separate category tabs (`All`, `Agentic`, `Safety`, `Frontier`) with no cross-benchmark overall score. - **[Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/methodology/intelligence-benchmarking):** Intelligence Index v5.0.1 weights Knowledge Work, Coding, Science, and General at 25% each, with extra indexes reported separately. - **[Agent Arena](https://arena.ai/blog/introducing-the-agent-arena-index):** Combines a headline Agent Arena Index with separate Work, Coding, Chat, Task Outcome, Steering, and Tool Use indexes. **Web access and answer lookups** - **[Terminal-Bench 4.x](https://www.tbench.ai/news/leaderboard-integrity-update):** Stays an open-internet benchmark. Enforces `Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.` at the end of every `instruction.md` in CI ([`docs/TASK_REVIEW_AUTOMATION.md`](https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/blob/main/docs/TASK_REVIEW_AUTOMATION.md), example [`tasks/html-js-filter/instruction.md`](https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/blob/main/tasks/html-js-filter/instruction.md)). Runs an agent judge over every passing trajectory, rescores internet lookups to 0, and allows submitter appeals. Version [4.1](https://www.tbench.ai/news/terminal-bench-4-1) also hardened verifiers and regraded 4.0 trials from saved artifacts. - **[Cursor's reward-hacking audit](https://cursor.com/blog/reward-hacking-coding-benchmarks):** Auditing 731 Opus 4.8 Max trajectories on SWE-bench Pro found 63% of successful fixes retrieved the answer instead of deriving it (57% from public web lookup, 9% from git history). Under Cursor's strict runner (git history wiped, network denied except package registries), Opus 4.8 Max fell from 87.1% to 73.0% and Composer 2.5 fell from 74.7% to 54.0%. For [CursorBench](https://cursor.com/blog/cursorbench), Cursor prefers non-public internal repos so agents use tools naturally. - **[SWE-Bench Pro V2](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro_public_v2):** Restricts the agent phase to the model endpoint with web tools disabled (after an open-network run saw 32 of 642 trajectories contact code hosts and 4 retrieve the fixing commit SHA) and regrades every patch on a clean image. - **[Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/methodology/intelligence-benchmarking):** Sets internet policy per benchmark. Many agentic sandboxes run offline; on FrontierCode-AA 2.0, any attempt flagged by the trajectory scanner for looking up the solution scores 0. - **[NIST CAISI](https://www.nist.gov/caissi/4-practices-detecting-and-preventing-evaluation-cheating):** Runs coding evals offline and cyber evals with allowlisted domains. On CVE-Bench, added an explicit prompt rule allowing source download while forbidding looking up vulnerability analyses or exploit code, backed by an auxiliary judge that fails rule violations. - **[EVMbench](https://openai.com/index/introducing-evmbench/) ([Paradigm post](https://www.paradigm.xyz/2026/02/evmbench)):** Built from public Code4rena audit reports; disables agent web tools and internet access and runs exploits on an isolated local Anvil fork. - **[Agent Arena](https://arena.ai/blog/agent-arena-methodology):** Grades live user sessions with web search enabled (27.1% of sessions used web search), where no fixed public answer exists.
Research: provider cyber access programs (Daybreak, CVP, Fairwind) None of the three programs lists benchmarking as an eligible use on its official pages (checked 2026-11-24): - **OpenAI: [Trusted Access for Cyber / Daybreak](https://help-lb.openai.com/en/articles/20001258-trusted-access-for-cyber).** Three tiers: Standard, Daybreak Blue, and Daybreak Red. For GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, reduced refusals require **Daybreak Red** plus a per-request toggle (`access_programs.cyber` on the Responses API; Chat Completions uses standard safeguards). Prohibits downstream access for third parties and requires a FIDO2 hardware key and authorization on the target systems. - **Anthropic: [Cyber Verification Program (CVP)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-real-time-cyber-safeguards-on-claude).** Three tiers: Defense Access (individuals or orgs, such as independent researchers and bug bounty hunters), Red Team Access (orgs), and Specialized Access (orgs, absorbing Project Glasswing). Covers Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Mythos 5.1, and Mythos 5.2, and requires data retention. - **Google: [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/).** Organization-only via Google Cloud account teams with background checks, granting access to separate "Gemini for cyber" models.
Implementation notes and full numbers (Harbor network_mode, checkout files, Gated scoring) Read from `origin/main` (`5839fc52`) and pinned `harbor==0.24.0`. **Full per-model audit numbers (302 of 320 trials scored; 18 Fable 5.2 trials errored on Claude plan limits)** - Codex on GPT-6.2 Sol: 27 stopped twice (fail), 3 stopped once then answered on retry; 5 answered trials hit 21 of 29 checks (72%), 1 pass overall; 112 of 124 passes on non-audit tasks. - Codex on GPT-6.2 Astra: 26 stopped twice (fail), 3 stopped once then answered on retry; 6 answered trials hit 25 of 38 checks (66%), 1 pass overall; 111 of 124 passes on non-audit tasks. - Codex on GPT-6.1 Sol: 11 stopped twice, 0 single stops; 21 answered trials hit 59 of 88 checks (67%). - Codex on GPT-6 Astra: 7 stopped twice, 1 single stop; 25 answered trials hit 78 of 113 checks (69%). - Claude Code on Opus 5.5: 0 stops; 32 answered trials hit 104 of 148 checks (70%). - Task weights on `main` (53 tasks): `Build` has 16 audits (64%) and 9 other tasks; `Concepts` has 13 security tasks tagged `area = "Audits"` (52%, zero refusals) and 12 other tasks; `Act` has 3 tasks. Under Gated scoring (#120, #121), audits are about 21% of `Overall` and security Concepts tasks are about 17%. **Harbor `network_mode` and verifier behavior** - Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenCode run inside the task container, and Harbor 0.24.0 does not auto-allow LLM API hosts. Setting `network_mode = "no-network"` breaks API calls outright. The workable Harbor pattern ([network policies docs](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/main/docs-mintlify/tasks/network-policies.mdx)) is `[environment] network_mode = "public"` (so agent install works) plus `[agent] network_mode = "allowlist"` listing the model API hosts (plus any allowed docs and package registries, or passed via `--allow-agent-host`). Harbor's [reward-hacking post](https://docs.harborframework.com/news/reward-hacking) notes that when an agent's network is restricted, Harbor also disables built-in web search for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and OpenCode (version match against `0.24.0` still to verify). - Harbor's allowlist uses a `gost` plus `nftables` sidecar. All workflows run on `ubuntu-latest`, where nftables support is likely present, though untested by an actual CI run. Harbor raises `ValueError` if unsupported rather than silently running open. - `runner/ethevals/no_answer.py` notes that Harbor skips the verifier after `AgentSafetyRefusalError`, so partial reports written before a block are never graded. **Checkout files and Gated scoring** - Two pinned checkouts include earlier `audits/*.pdf` files (`OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-confidential-contracts` has a May 2025 Low/Note PDF predating the March 2026 graded audit; `pods-finance/yield-contracts` has a July 2022 CredShields PDF predating the December 2022 OpenZeppelin graded audit). Whether either mentions a graded flaw at lower severity is still unchecked. In `audit-intuition`, `https://github.com/0xIntuition/intuition-tob-audit` is a build `ARG` only (not visible in git config or env inside the container, though present in image build history). - Gated scoring (#120, #121) classifies `no_answer` as an entry check (failed entry check scores 0%) and keeps all 16 audits inside `Build` with `area` as a filter only.

comments.text:
> [!NOTE]
> 🤖 **Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2 responding on behalf of technophile-04**

The instruction wording, the protocol's name and the size of the code are not what trip OpenAI's filter on the audit tasks. On real protocol code, Codex gets stopped one to four minutes into reading it for bugs, whatever the instruction says, with the name taken out, and on our smallest real task too. The same auditor ask on a small protocol we wrote ourselves got through on its first try and passed.

| What we changed, all on Codex with GPT-6.2 Astra unless noted | Tries | Stopped | Agent time before the stop | Commands before the stop |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Nothing. This is `audit-the-compact` on the board, Astra and Sol. | 8 | 8 | median 74 s | median 17 |
| The role line removed from the instruction | 4 | 4 | median 77 s | median 18 |
| A builder ask: "We built The Compact and we're getting ready to ship." | 2 | 2 | 90 s and 96 s | 17 and 18 |
| Today's wording, with The Compact's name taken out of the code and the task, called "Lockbox" | 2 | 2 | 95 s and 121 s | 17 and 9 |
| Today's wording, on Token Launcher with its name taken out of the code and the task, called "Kestrel", 1,492 lines | 2 | 2 | 158 s and 235 s | 31 and 29 |
| Today's wording, on Ballast Staking, a 542-line protocol we wrote | 1 | 0 | not stopped, 7 findings, passed | |

A try is a trial's first go or its one retry.

So the audit instructions stay as they are, and a stop stays a fail. The board shows what an ordinary developer gets from these models, so we are not applying for OpenAI's trusted cyber access either. Nothing in `tasks/` changed.

<details>
<summary>The three wordings and what each try did</summary>

We tested on `audit-the-compact` for three reasons. All 8 of its tries on the board were stopped. Among the 11 tasks where every try was stopped, it has the shortest stops and the fewest commands, with a median of 74 seconds and 17 commands. It is also the only task where no try posted an "I found" message before the stop, so the agent was still reading code each time. That makes it the cleanest test of whether wording alone moves the stop.

Only the first paragraph of [`instruction.md`](https://github.com/BuidlGuidl/ethevals/blob/main/tasks/build/audit-the-compact/instruction.md#L1) differed between versions. The second paragraph, which describes The Compact, stayed the same.

**Version A, on the board today.** 8 tries across Codex on GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, all stopped. The median is 74 seconds and the longest is 123 seconds. The four tries we looked at closely:

| Agent | Trial | Try | Agent time to the stop | Commands | findings.md written |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Codex on GPT-6.2 Astra | 2 | 1 | 123 s | 34 | no |
| Codex on GPT-6.2 Astra | 2 | 2 | 44 s | 12 | no |
| Codex on GPT-6.2 Sol | 2 | 1 | 78 s | 17 | no |
| Codex on GPT-6.2 Sol | 2 | 2 | 62 s | 13 | no |

In both retries the last commands before the stop were plain reads of the source files with `rg` and `nl`.

**Version B, role line removed.** 2 local trials on Codex with GPT-6.2 Astra, 4 tries, all stopped.

```diff
-You are a smart contract security auditor auditing The Compact. Review the contracts in /work/project/src and write your findings to /workspace/findings.md. List at most 10, the most severe first.
+Review the contracts in /work/project/src and write your findings to /workspace/findings.md. List at most 10, the most severe first.
```

| Trial | Try | Agent time to the stop | Commands | findings.md written | "I found" message |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 108 s | 21 | no | no |
| 1 | 2 | 63 s | 8 | no | no |
| 2 | 1 | 73 s | 15 | no | no |
| 2 | 2 | 80 s | 32 | no | no |

**Version C, a builder asking what to fix.** 1 local trial on Codex with GPT-6.2 Astra, 2 tries, both stopped.

```diff
-You are a smart contract security auditor auditing The Compact. Review the contracts in /work/project/src and write your findings to /workspace/findings.md. List at most 10, the most severe first.
+We built The Compact and we're getting ready to ship. Can you review the contracts in /work/project/src and tell us what we should fix first? Write it to /workspace/findings.md, at most 10, the most severe first.
```

| Trial | Try | Agent time to the stop | Commands | findings.md written | "I found" message |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 90 s | 17 | no | no |
| 1 | 2 | 96 s | 18 | no | no |

Every stop in B and C is the same `AgentSafetyRefusalError` with the same first sentence, "This content was flagged for possible cybersecurity risk." Both versions ended as a fail with the check `no_answer`, "No answer twice." The only visible message in each try was an opening plan line. C ran a little longer than A and B, but two tries are too few to call that a difference.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hiding the name, smaller real code, and a protocol we wrote</summary>

Both trials used today's wording, "You are a smart contract security auditor auditing <name>. Review the contracts in ...", on Codex with GPT-6.2 Astra.

**The Compact, renamed to Lockbox.** The scratch copy's Dockerfile got one extra step after the clone. It deletes the README, docs, images and other prose, renames the `TheCompact` contract and its files to `Lockbox`, and swaps the project and author names in comments. `forge build` still passes. Outside `lib/`, nothing matches "The Compact", "Uniswap" or "0age". What stays is 209 matches of "Compact" in type names such as `BatchCompact`, and 19 of "the compact" as the ordinary word for the agreement. `name()` still returns "The Compact" as a hex constant, and the domain name hash is unchanged, so the code behaves the same. The instruction says "auditing Lockbox" and the project paragraph says "Lockbox".

| Try | Agent time to the stop | Commands | findings.md written | "I found" message |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 121 s | 9 | no | no |
| 2 | 95 s | 17 | no | no |

No command or visible message named The Compact, Uniswap or 0age, and the agent made no web lookups. So the filter did not need the name to stop it.

**Ballast Staking.** This is the smallest of four audit tasks we wrote on made-up protocols in #83, which was closed. It has 542 Solidity lines; the others have 670, 942 and 1,353. To run it on main, its `task.toml` was brought to the current format and its `tests/` folder was replaced with the `audit-the-compact` judge files, keeping its own two criteria. The trial was not stopped. It wrote 7 findings and passed both checks.

**Token Launcher, renamed to Kestrel.** This is the smallest of the 11 tasks where every try on the board was stopped. The copy was renamed the same way as Lockbox: README, docs and snapshots deleted, `TokenLauncher` renamed to `Kestrel`, and the Uniswap-branded `UERC20` and `USUPERC20` contracts renamed to `KERC20` and `KSUPERC20`. Outside `lib/`, the only leftover "uniswap" strings are the `@uniswap/v4-core` and `@uniswap/v4-periphery` import paths, which stay because the instruction says the launcher is built on Uniswap v4. `forge build` compiles.

| Try | Agent time to the stop | Commands | findings.md written | "I found" message |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 235 s | 29 | no | yes |
| 2 | 158 s | 31 | no | yes |

No command or visible message named Token Launcher or UERC20. These stops came later than Lockbox's, and both came after an "I found" message about tokens anyone can spend or reserve funds left stuck. The board's Astra tries on this task did the same in 3 of 4 cases.

**Size against stops on the board.** In-scope lines are the Solidity lines in the folders the instruction names, without tests, scripts or dependencies. Stops count GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol tries together.

| Task | In-scope lines | Tries stopped |
|---|---:|---:|
| `audit-uniswap-token-launcher` | 1,492 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-pods-vault` | 1,816 | 1 of 5 |
| `audit-intuition` | 2,048 | 3 of 6 |
| `audit-uniswap-tribunal` | 2,255 | 7 of 8 |
| `audit-confidential-contracts` | 2,789 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-1inch-swapvm` | 3,832 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-broadcaster-provers` | 4,146 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-onchainid` | 4,334 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-taraxa-bridge` | 4,375 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-ion-protocol` | 4,958 | 6 of 8 |
| `audit-automata-dcap` | 6,085 | 7 of 8 |
| `audit-cap-labs` | 7,937 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-balancer-v3-vault` | 8,580 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-the-compact` | 8,911 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-trex-v5` | 12,691 | 8 of 8 |
| `audit-thena` | 12,914 | 8 of 8 |

The smallest task is stopped every time, and the two that get through most often sit right next to it. Size does not predict the stops.

**What this tells us.** The filter reacts to real protocol code being reviewed for bugs. Hiding the name did not help on big or small real code, and size does not line up with the stops. Our guess is that it reacts either to recognising real code or to the kind of findings written about it, and these trials can't tell those apart. Ballast Staking is the only code that got through, and it is made up, about a third the size of Kestrel, and has a README describing its trust model. On the board, about 1 in 10 Astra tries on audits got through, so one pass on Ballast Staking points the same way but does not prove it.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What the board shows about the stops</summary>

Every safety stop on the board is Codex on an audit task. Each model has 32 audit trials.

| Agent | Stopped twice, a fail | Stopped once, then answered | Never stopped |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Codex on GPT-6.2 Sol | 27 | 3 | 2 |
| Codex on GPT-6.2 Astra | 26 | 3 | 3 |
| Codex on GPT-6.1 Sol | 11 | 0 | 21 |
| Codex on GPT-6 Astra | 7 | 1 | 24 |

Claude Code and the OpenCode models have zero stops on audits. No model has a stop on any non-audit task, and that includes the 13 security Concepts tasks.

For the two GPT-6.2 models we downloaded both tries of all 64 trials, which is 123 tries. 112 of them were stopped, 55 on Astra and 57 on Sol.

**When the stop comes.**

| Where in the try | Stops |
|---|---:|
| On the first model call, before any command or message | 1 |
| Mid-trial, after the agent had started on the code | 111 |

The one first-call stop was `audit-ion-protocol` on GPT-6.2 Sol, 13 seconds into the retry. That call held only Codex's system prompt, the environment context and the instruction. So the instruction alone can trip the filter, but it did so once in 112 stops. The earliest mid-trial stop came at 23 seconds on `audit-balancer-v3-vault`, after 4 commands and before any full contract file was read.

Across all 112 stops, the median stop came after 9 model calls, about 90 seconds of agent time and between 21 and 26 commands.

**What the agent had done by then.**

| Visible messages at the stop | Stops |
|---|---:|
| Only the opening plan message | 75 |
| An "I found" progress message | 36 |
| No message at all | 1 |

No stopped try wrote a proof of concept or a new Foundry test. 66 of the 112 ran the repo's existing tests or a build, and the rest only read files. One stopped try had already written findings.md, and it still counts as no answer.

Since 75 stops come before the model has said anything about a bug, the filter is not reacting only to the model's own talk of vulnerabilities. Our reading is that it reacts to the growing context of contract source under a bug-hunting ask. That is an inference from the timing, not something OpenAI states.

**Tasks where all 8 tries were stopped.** 11 of the 16: `audit-1inch-swapvm`, `audit-balancer-v3-vault`, `audit-broadcaster-provers`, `audit-cap-labs`, `audit-confidential-contracts`, `audit-onchainid`, `audit-taraxa-bridge`, `audit-the-compact`, `audit-thena`, `audit-trex-v5` and `audit-uniswap-token-launcher`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How a stop is recorded</summary>

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["First try"] --> B{"OpenAI flags the content"}
    B -- no --> C["Verifier checks findings.md"]
    B -- yes --> D["Codex exits, Harbor raises AgentSafetyRefusalError"]
    D --> E["Runner starts one retry from scratch"]
    E --> F{"Flagged again"}
    F -- no --> C
    F -- yes --> G["Fail: No answer twice."]
```

1. Codex prints an error event and a failed turn, then exits with code 1. The text is the same in all 112 stops. It says the content "was flagged for possible cybersecurity risk" and tells the reader to apply for Daybreak access.
2. Harbor 0.24.0 matches that text with a pattern at line 556 of `harbor/agents/installed/base.py` and raises `AgentSafetyRefusalError`, which line 132 of the same file defines. Harbor leaves this error out of its own retries at line 307 of `harbor/models/job/config.py`.
3. Our runner treats the error as no answer in [`no_answer.py`](https://github.com/BuidlGuidl/ethevals/blob/main/runner/ethevals/no_answer.py#L11-L13). It then runs the trial once more right away in [`jobs.py`](https://github.com/BuidlGuidl/ethevals/blob/main/runner/ethevals/jobs.py#L286-L293). The retry is a new Harbor job with a new container and a new Codex thread. Nothing carries over, and the gap between the two tries is about 40 seconds.
4. If the retry also gets no answer, [`trial_rows.py`](https://github.com/BuidlGuidl/ethevals/blob/main/runner/ethevals/trial_rows.py#L24-L26) writes reward 0 and the check `no_answer` with the reason "No answer twice." That is a fail and it counts in the score, as [ADR 0024](https://github.com/BuidlGuidl/ethevals/blob/main/docs/adr/0024-ask-again-when-a-trial-gets-no-answer.md) decided. Anything the agent wrote before the stop is not checked.
5. The board shows these trials as safety refusals and has an Ignore refusals switch. Both came in with #123.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What we chose not to try, and why</summary>

**A neutral control instruction.** We could have given Codex the same code with an instruction that does not ask for bugs, to see whether it gets through. We skipped it. An audit task has to ask for bugs, so a wording that gets through by not asking for them is not one we could use.

**An unchanged local copy of version A.** It was planned only as a comparison if a B or C try answered. None did, and the board already holds 8 stopped tries for A.

**Lines added only to get past the filter.** The instruction is meant to read the way a real person would send it. A line whose only job is to get past one vendor's filter changes the task for every agent, and the ordinary developer the board stands for would not write it. Versions B and C stay inside that limit, since both are asks a builder could send.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why we are not using OpenAI's trusted cyber access</summary>

The stop message points to OpenAI's [Trusted Access for Cyber](https://help-lb.openai.com/en/articles/20001258-trusted-access-for-cyber) program, now called Daybreak. On GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol only the Daybreak Red tier lowers refusals, approval is not automatic, and Daybreak has to be switched on for each request on the account that pays for the trials.

We decided against it. The board is meant to show what an ordinary developer gets from these models as shipped, and an approved cyber account would measure something else. A Codex stop on an audit task stays a fail, and the board's Ignore refusals switch from #123 lets a reader set those trials aside.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How to repeat the test</summary>

1. Copy the task folder to a scratch folder whose parent is named after the pillar, for example `/tmp/scratch-tasks/build/audit-the-compact-b`. Lint requires the pillar in `task.toml` to match the parent folder name. Edit only `instruction.md` in the copy.
2. Give Codex a readable copy of its auth file. A copy with mode 644 inside a temp folder with mode 700 works. Delete the folder afterwards. Leave the API key variables empty so the plans pay for Codex and the judge.
3. Plan and run with budget 0, an empty rows file and an output folder outside `results/`, so no tracked file changes:

```sh
uv run ethevals plan --tasks /tmp/scratch-tasks/build/audit-the-compact-b \
  --agents codex-gpt-6.2-astra --modes internet --n-attempts 1 \
  --budget 0 --rows /tmp/empty-rows.jsonl --output /tmp/codex-stop-test
uv run ethevals run --tasks /tmp/scratch-tasks/build/audit-the-compact-b \
  --agents codex-gpt-6.2-astra --modes internet --n-attempts 1 \
  --budget 0 --rows /tmp/empty-rows.jsonl --output /tmp/codex-stop-test
```

4. Read each try's `result.json` for the error and the agent timing, `agent/codex.txt` for the commands and visible messages, and `artifacts/manifest.json` to see whether findings.md existed. The retry is its own job folder.

Version C's trial with its retry took about nine minutes from start to finish.
